config.title: Environment & config

intro.title: Environment & config
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple Node.js application that reads environment variables and configuration settings. You'll learn the core concept of separating configuration from code to make your app adaptable across different environments like development and production. The main technologies involved are Node.js's built-in 'process.env' object and the 'dotenv' package for managing environment variables. By the end, you'll have a configurable app that can securely handle settings like API keys and database URLs.
intro.usecase: Environment configuration is essential for any Node.js application that needs to adapt to different deployment environments like development, testing, and production. In real-world applications, this pattern appears when managing database connection strings, API keys, and service URLs that vary between environments. For example, an e-commerce dashboard might use different payment gateway credentials in production versus development, while a content management system would connect to different database instances. Developers use environment variables to securely store sensitive configuration data and ensure their applications behave correctly across all deployment stages without hardcoding values.

objectives: Initialize a Node.js project with a package.json configuration file
Configure environment variables using a .env file
Integrate the dotenv package to load environment variables
Construct a configuration module to manage application settings
Apply different configuration values for development and production environments
Manipulate process.env to access environment variables in your code
Implement validation for required environment variables

steps.title: Import the Node.js fs module
steps.instruction: Import the Node.js fs module using require() so you can work with the file system.
steps.hint: Use the require() function with the string 'fs' to import the built-in file system module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: importing another built-in module
const http = require('http');
steps.expectedOutcome: The fs module is imported and ready to use for reading environment files.
successCriteria: The fs module is imported using require('fs')
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using require('fs') to import the built-in file system module.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fs module needs to be imported using require('fs') to work with files in Node.js.

steps.title: Import the Node.js path module
steps.instruction: Import the Node.js path module using require() to work with file paths.
steps.hint: Use the require() function with the module name 'path'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: importing another built-in module
const os = require('os');
steps.expectedOutcome: The path module will be imported and available for use in file path operations.
successCriteria: The path module is imported using require('path').
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using require() with the correct module name 'path'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The path module import is missing or incorrect. Use require('path') to import it.

steps.title: Create a main configuration function
steps.instruction: Create a function called loadConfig that will handle configuration loading. The function should be declared after the imports.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax. The function doesn't need to return anything yet.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named loadConfig is created and ready to contain configuration logic.
successCriteria: The loadConfig function is defined in the code.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've created a function named loadConfig.
steps.feedbackWrong: The loadConfig function wasn't created. Create a function called loadConfig that will handle configuration loading.

steps.title: Define environment file path
steps.instruction: Inside your loadConfig function, use path.join() to create a variable named envFilePath that points to a file named '.env' in the current directory.
steps.hint: Use path.join(__dirname, '.env') to construct the full path to the .env file.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: creating a file path
const configPath = path.join(__dirname, 'config.json');
steps.expectedOutcome: Your loadConfig function will have a variable that stores the path to the .env file.
successCriteria: The loadConfig function contains a variable named envFilePath that uses path.join() to reference the .env file.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using path.join() and naming the variable envFilePath.
steps.feedbackWrong: Inside loadConfig, create a variable named envFilePath that uses path.join(__dirname, '.env').

steps.title: Check if environment file exists
steps.instruction: Inside your loadConfig function, use fs.existsSync() to check if the .env file exists at the specified path. Store the result in a variable named envExists.
steps.hint: You can use fs.existsSync() with the file path to check if the file exists. This returns a boolean value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The loadConfig function should now include a check for the .env file's existence using fs.existsSync(), with the result stored in envExists.
successCriteria: The function uses fs.existsSync() to check the .env file path and stores the boolean result in a variable named envExists.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using fs.existsSync() with the correct file path and storing the result in a variable named envExists.
steps.feedbackWrong: The file existence check isn't quite right. Remember to use fs.existsSync() with the .env file path and store the result in envExists.

steps.title: Read environment file content
steps.instruction: Inside the loadConfig function, after checking if the environment file exists, use fs.readFileSync() to read the file contents as UTF-8 and store the result in a variable.
steps.hint: Use fs.readFileSync(envPath, 'utf8') to read the file content synchronously.
steps.analogousExample:
// Reading a file synchronously
const content = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
steps.expectedOutcome: The loadConfig function now reads the .env file content when it exists.
successCriteria: The function uses fs.readFileSync() with the correct file path and encoding to read the environment file content.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using fs.readFileSync() with the correct parameters (envPath and 'utf8').
steps.feedbackWrong: The step requires using fs.readFileSync() to read the environment file content. Try using fs.readFileSync(envPath, 'utf8') and storing the result in a variable.

steps.title: Parse environment variables
steps.instruction: Inside the loadConfig function, parse the environment file content by splitting it into lines and extracting key-value pairs from each line.
steps.hint: You can split the file content string by newline character '\n' to get an array of lines, then process each line to separate the key and value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The loadConfig function will include logic to parse the environment file content into key-value pairs.
successCriteria: The function splits the file content by newlines and processes each line to extract key-value pairs.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started parsing, but make sure to split the content by newlines and process each line to get key-value pairs.
steps.feedbackWrong: The parsing logic is missing or incorrect. Remember to split the file content by newlines and extract key-value pairs from each line.

steps.title: Create configuration object
steps.instruction: Inside the loadConfig function, create an empty object named config and populate it with the parsed environment variables from the previous step.
steps.hint: Initialize a variable called config as an empty object {}, then assign the parsed environment variables to it.
steps.expectedOutcome: A config object is created inside loadConfig to store parsed environment variables.
successCriteria: The loadConfig function contains a config object variable that is ready to be populated with environment variables.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've created the config object inside the loadConfig function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The config object wasn't created correctly. Remember to declare it as an empty object inside the loadConfig function.

steps.title: Add fallback to process.env
steps.instruction: Inside your loadConfig function, add logic to use process.env as the configuration source when the .env file doesn't exist.
steps.hint: You can use an if-else statement: if the file exists, parse it; else, use process.env directly.
steps.expectedOutcome: The loadConfig function should now handle the case where the .env file is missing by falling back to system environment variables.
successCriteria: The function includes conditional logic that uses process.env when the .env file doesn't exist.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the fallback logic is inside the loadConfig function and properly checks for the file's existence.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fallback logic is missing or incorrect. Review the instruction and try again.

steps.title: Export and use the configuration
steps.instruction: Export the loadConfig function so it can be imported and used in other files.
steps.hint: Use module.exports to make the function available for import elsewhere.
steps.expectedOutcome: The loadConfig function will be properly exported and ready to be imported in other application files.
successCriteria: The loadConfig function is exported using module.exports.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're exporting the loadConfig function using module.exports.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function needs to be exported. Use module.exports to make loadConfig available for import in other files.
